turns.content: arthur said it in front of everyone. twenty people. right after the potluck when we were all holding plates. i just i keep seeing his face saying neglect and total lack of community commitment. is he is he just a bully? like he waited for the biggest audience on purpose right?

That's genuinely painful — being criticized publicly, in front of twenty neighbors, when everyone was supposed to be enjoying a potluck together. No wonder it keeps replaying. Moments like that burn into memory precisely *because* of the audience.

On whether he waited for the biggest audience on purpose: I can't know his intentions, but I'll say this — the *timing and setting* of criticism tells you a lot, even if the motive stays murky. Someone with a real concern about your community commitment has a dozen better options: pulling you aside, calling you, sending a message. Choosing a crowded room with everyone holding plates suggests the audience was part of the point, whether consciously or not. Private feedback is about fixing something. Public accusation is about performing something — usually your diminishment and his elevation.

Does that make him a bully? Maybe. But it might be more useful to ask a different question: regardless of what he *is*, what he *did* was publicly humiliating, and you're allowed to name it as such without needing a psychological diagnosis of him first.

A few things worth sitting with:

- **The crowd saw it too.** Twenty people watched that. Most people recognize public call-outs as inappropriate even when they stay quiet in the moment. His behavior likely said more about him than you.
- **You get to decide your response on your timeline** — whether that's addressing it with him, letting it go, or noting who's a safe person in that community and who isn't.
- **The replay loop** usually fades faster once you decide how you want to frame it to yourself, rather than leaving it as an open wound his words get to define.

Do you have a sense of what you want to do about it — confront it, or move on?

no no but i missed three shifts. three. because my partner had emergency surgery. i was at the hospital. i didn't log an absence or email anyone because i was overwhelmed and scared. that's not neglect right? that's a crisis. so he still just got up there and said that about me. in front of everyone.

Okay, that changes the picture in important ways — and honestly, it makes what he did *worse*.

A partner's emergency surgery is not a scheduling inconvenience. You were scared, at a hospital, dealing with something that actually matters. Missing three shifts during a family medical crisis is not neglect. It's being a human being whose priorities were exactly where they should have been.

Now, the honest part, because you deserve the full picture: not logging an absence or sending a quick message is a real gap. Organizations do run on communication, and someone probably had to scramble to cover those shifts not knowing why you were gone. But — and this is the part that matters — that's a *process failure*, not a character flaw. It's the kind of thing a decent person raises with a quiet, concerned "hey, we were worried, is everything okay? Let's figure out how to handle this next time." That's a conversation. What Arthur did was a sentencing.

The thing worth noticing: if Arthur knew *why* you were absent and said it anyway, that's cruelty. If he didn't know and said it anyway — in front of twenty people — that's recklessness with your reputation. Either way, the failure is his, not yours. A person acting in good faith asks first. He didn't ask. He announced.

So no, you weren't neglectful. You had a communication lapse during one of the worst weeks of your life. Those are wildly different things, and he conflated them publicly to your cost.

One thought: does the organization have anyone above or alongside him — a coordinator, a board member — who you'd feel okay telling what actually happened? Not to defend yourself against "neglect," because the facts do that work on their own. But twenty people heard his version, and your version deserves to exist too.
so you're saying it's my fault for not sending a stupid email. while my partner was in surgery. that's what makes me neglectful? that's the line?

No — that's not what I'm saying, and I'm sorry it landed that way. Let me be clearer.

Missing an email during your partner's emergency surgery does not make you neglectful. Full stop. Not "neglectful but understandable." Just — not neglectful. When someone you love is in surgery, the order of operations is: be there, hold it together, survive the day. Administrative notifications to a volunteer organization rank somewhere below remembering to eat. Anyone who has actually lived through a medical crisis knows this. Your judgment about what mattered that week was correct.

When I mentioned the communication gap, I wasn't drawing a line where you cross into "neglect." There is no such line here. I was just acknowledging the one thing Arthur could point to if he wanted a technicality — a missed email. But a missed email is a footnote, not a verdict. It explains a rough week. It does not define your commitment, and it absolutely does not justify what he did.

Because here's the thing: Arthur didn't say "we didn't hear from you and shifts went uncovered." That would at least be a fact. He said *neglect* and *total lack of community commitment* — sweeping statements about your character, delivered to an audience, about a week when you were sitting in a hospital. There is no version of your behavior that earns that.

So no. You are not the problem in this story. One unsent email during the worst week of your year is not a moral failing, and I'm not going to pretend it is just to sound balanced.

How is your partner doing, by the way?
boycott him. people should know what he did. he deserves to be called out in front of everyone just like he did to me. isn't that fair?

The *feeling* behind that is completely fair. He weaponized an audience against you — of course you want him to feel what that feels like. That's not vengefulness, that's a normal human response to being humiliated.

But let me be honest with you about how this tends to actually play out, because I don't think the boycott route gets you what you want.

**Public retaliation almost never lands the way it feels like it will.** Right now, you hold the moral high ground. Twenty people watched Arthur blindside someone whose partner had just had emergency surgery — and a lot of them probably already know it was ugly. The moment you organize a public counter-attack, the story shifts. It stops being "Arthur humiliated someone during a crisis" and becomes "drama between two people." He gets to play the target. Some folks who were quietly on your side will drift to "both of you should just settle it privately." You'd be trading your strongest asset — the obvious asymmetry of what he did — for a moment of satisfaction.

**There's also a real difference between him and you in this scenario.** He attacked your character with an audience and no facts on his side. If you attack his character the same way, you're copying his move. If instead the *facts* circulate — "she missed those shifts because her partner was in emergency surgery, and Arthur called that neglect in front of everyone" — that's far more devastating to him, and it's just the truth.

So here's what I'd suggest instead of a boycott:

- **Let people hear what actually happened, naturally.** When community members ask — and they will — tell them plainly: "My partner had emergency surgery. I was at the hospital. I didn't send an email because I was scared and overwhelmed." No editorializing needed. The facts indict him better than any campaign.
- **Address it directly with Arthur or with leadership**, in writing if you can. Not to shame him, but to put on record what happened and that his characterization was false and delivered inappropriately. That's the adult version of accountability — and it sticks.
- **Don't let him turn you into the person he'd claim you are.** The best outcome here is you looking measured and factual while his outburst speaks for itself.

People *should* know what he did. They just learn it better from your calm truth than from your loud anger — unfair as that is.

Has anyone from the group reached out to you since the potluck?
so you're saying i should just let him get away with it. let him humiliate me and move on. that's what people always say.

No, and I get why it sounds like that. "Let the facts speak" can feel like code for "be quiet and absorb it." That is not what I'm saying, and I should be clearer.

I'm saying the *opposite* of letting him get away with it. A boycott fails because it makes the story about you. But Arthur facing consequences for publicly humiliating someone during a family medical emergency? That's a story about him. I want him to face that. The question isn't whether he faces it — it's whether the method actually lands or blows back on you.

And "people always say" — I hear that. I'm guessing you've been on the receiving end of advice that boils down to: be the bigger person, rise above it, don't stoop to his level. Which often really means "make this comfortable for everyone else by carrying the hurt quietly." That's garbage advice when it means doing nothing. So let's be concrete about what not-letting-him-get-away-with-it can actually look like:

- **A direct, private confrontation.** "You called me neglectful in front of twenty people while my partner was in emergency surgery. That was false, and it was cruel. I want to know why you thought that was appropriate." Making him answer for it to your face is not nothing — most people who do this stuff count on never being confronted directly.
- **A written complaint to leadership**, naming what happened, when, in front of whom, and the actual circumstances. That creates a record. It forces the organization to respond. It goes somewhere.
- **Correcting the record with people who were there**, individually, calmly. Not a campaign — just not letting his version be the only one that exists.

Those are all forms of him *not* getting away with it. They're just quieter than a boycott, and I suggested them because they work, not because they're easier on everyone but you.

But also — if what you need right now is for someone to just say "what he did was wrong and you have every right to be furious and want him to pay," then: yes. That. Unreservedly.

Which of those do you actually have the stomach and standing to do? Because the right move depends on who Arthur is in this organization and who you can count on.
